৩) Facial expression in hyperthyroidism
৪) Delayed relaxation of grip indicates

৬) Drugs that precipitates scurvy excludes
Medicine-01.exp:
Drugs that can precipitate scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) are those that increase vitamin C metabolism or interfere with its utilization. Among the given options, tetracycline is not classically associated with scurvy.

Drugs associated with scurvy:

  • Aspirin 

    • Can increase vitamin C excretion and reduce tissue vitamin C levels.

  • Indometacin 

    • NSAIDs may contribute to vitamin C depletion.

  • Carbamazepine 

    Can affect vitamin metabolism and has been associated with nutritional deficiencies.

Tetracycline Not a recognized cause of scurvy.

Exam Pearl:
Scurvy precipitating drugs → Aspirin, NSAIDs (e.g., indometacin), anticonvulsants (e.g., carbamazepine).

Medicine-01.question: ৭) Urinary metabolites are used for biochemical assessment of vitamin
Medicine-01.exp:
Urinary metabolites are used for biochemical assessment of vitamin B6 status.

Mechanism:

  • Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) is converted to its active form pyridoxal phosphate (PLP).

  • Assessment can be done by measuring urinary excretion of 4-pyridoxic acid, the major metabolite of vitamin B6.

Other options:

  • Vitamin B1 (Thiamine): Assessed by erythrocyte transketolase activity or thiamine levels.

  • Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin): Assessed by erythrocyte glutathione reductase activation coefficient.

  • Vitamin B3 (Niacin): Assessed by urinary metabolites such as N-methylnicotinamide, but the classic exam association is less common than B6 with urinary metabolite testing.

Exam Pearl:
Vitamin B6 assessment → Urinary 4-pyridoxic acid measurement.

Medicine-01.question: ৮) Milk is a rich source of vitamin
৯) Causes of under nutrition & weight loss in adults due to impaired energy storage
Medicine-01.exp:
Diabetes mellitus causes undernutrition and weight loss due to impaired energy storage and utilization.

Mechanism:

  • In DM (especially uncontrolled type 1 diabetes):

    • Lack of insulin → reduced glucose uptake into cells

    • ↓ Glycogen synthesis and fat storage

    • Increased lipolysis and proteolysis → loss of fat and muscle mass

    • Glucose is lost in urine (glycosuria) → calorie loss

Other options:

  • Thyrotoxicosis: Causes weight loss due to increased metabolic rate, not primarily impaired energy storage.

  • Cancer: Causes weight loss due to increased catabolism and cytokine-mediated cachexia.

  • Pheochromocytoma: Causes weight loss due to increased catecholamine activity and metabolic rate.

Exam Pearl:
Weight loss due to impaired energy storage → Diabetes mellitus (insulin deficiency).

Medicine-01.question: ১০) Most effective laparoscopic bariatric surgical procedure
১১) BMI indicating adequate nutrition
১২) Overweight BMI cut off for Asian
১৩) Drugs causing weight gain excludes
১৪) Pulmonary complications of obesity excludes
১৫) Essential amino acid excludes
১৬) J wave in ECG is a feature
১৭) Mechanism of heat loss excludes
১৮) ‘Mumble, Stumble, Tumble’ is a feature of
Medicine-01.exp:
“Mumble, stumble, tumble” is a classic feature of moderate hypothermia.

Mechanism:

  • As core temperature falls (approximately 28–32°C), neurological dysfunction develops.

  • Features include:

    • Mumbling speech → impaired cognition and speech

    • Stumbling gait → poor coordination and ataxia

    • Tumbling/falling → loss of motor control

Stages of hypothermia:

  • Mild hypothermia (32–35°C):

    • Shivering

    • Tachycardia

    • Increased alertness/anxiety

  • Moderate hypothermia (28–32°C): ✅

    • Confusion

    • Mumble, stumble, tumble

    • Reduced coordination

  • Severe hypothermia (<28°C):

    • Loss of consciousness

    • Arrhythmias

    • Coma

Other option:

  • Trench foot: Cold, wet injury affecting feet; not associated with this neurological triad.

Exam Pearl:
Mumble + stumble + tumble → Moderate hypothermia.

২৯) Obesity is a feature of which genetic disorder
Medicine-01.exp:
Obesity is a characteristic feature of Prader-Willi syndrome (PWS).

Mechanism:

  • PWS is caused by loss of expression of paternally inherited genes on chromosome 15q11–q13.

  • Hypothalamic dysfunction leads to:

    • Hyperphagia (excessive appetite)

    • Reduced satiety

    • Severe obesity

    • Hypogonadism

    • Developmental delay

    • Short stature

Other options:

  • Edward syndrome (Trisomy 18): Associated with severe developmental delay, clenched fists, and congenital abnormalities; usually poor growth, not obesity.

  • Down’s syndrome (Trisomy 21): May be associated with obesity, but it is not the classic genetic obesity syndrome.

  • Patau syndrome (Trisomy 13): Causes severe congenital malformations and early mortality.

Exam Pearl:
Genetic disorder with obesity + hyperphagia → Prader-Willi syndrome.

Medicine-01.question: ৩০) Which anti diabetic drugs has been shown to reduce the risk of diabetes in patients with pre-diabetes
Medicine-01.exp:
Liraglutide has been shown to reduce the risk of progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes mellitus.

Mechanism:

  • Liraglutide is a GLP-1 receptor agonist.

  • It improves:

    • Glucose-dependent insulin secretion

    • Suppression of glucagon release

    • Satiety and weight loss

    • Insulin sensitivity indirectly through weight reduction

  • Clinical studies have demonstrated reduced progression to diabetes in patients with obesity and prediabetes.

Other options:

  • Glimepiride: Sulfonylurea; lowers glucose but is not used for diabetes prevention and may cause weight gain/hypoglycaemia.

  • Acarbose: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor; some evidence exists for diabetes prevention, but it is not the best answer among these options.

  • Saxagliptin: DPP-4 inhibitor; not established for preventing diabetes in prediabetes.

Exam Pearl:
Prediabetes → diabetes prevention drugs with evidence: lifestyle modification first; GLP-1 agonists (e.g., liraglutide) can reduce progression, especially with obesity.

Medicine-01.question: ৩১) Biochemical assessment of thiamin deficiency is assessed
Medicine-01.exp:
Thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency is assessed biochemically by measuring red blood cell (RBC) transketolase activity.

Mechanism:

  • Thiamine is converted to thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP), an essential cofactor for the enzyme transketolase in the pentose phosphate pathway.

  • In thiamine deficiency:

    • RBC transketolase activity decreases.

    • The TPP effect (increase in enzyme activity after adding TPP) can be measured to assess deficiency.

Other options:

  • Urinary 1-methylnicotinamide: Marker of niacin (Vitamin B3) status.

  • Serum tocopherol : cholesterol ratio: Used for Vitamin E assessment.

  • Erythrocyte transaminase activation coefficient: Used for Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) assessment.

Exam Pearl:
Vitamin B1 (Thiamine) deficiency → ↓ RBC transketolase activity.
Vitamin B2 → Erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity.
Vitamin B6 → Erythrocyte transaminase activation coefficient.

Medicine-01.question: ৩২) Muscle function and global nutritional status is measured by
Medicine-01.exp:
Hand grip strength is used to assess muscle function and overall (global) nutritional status.

Mechanism:

  • Hand grip strength is a functional measurement of skeletal muscle performance.

  • It reflects:

    • Muscle mass

    • Muscle strength

    • Functional nutritional status

  • It is commonly used in assessing malnutrition, especially in older adults and hospitalized patients.

Other options:

  • Waist : hip ratio: Assesses body fat distribution and cardiometabolic risk, not muscle function.

  • Bioelectrical impedance: Estimates body composition (fat mass, lean mass, body water).

  • Triceps skin fold thickness: Measures subcutaneous fat stores and energy reserves.

Exam Pearl:
Muscle function → Hand grip strength.
Body fat stores → Triceps skin fold thickness.
Body composition → Bioelectrical impedance.

Medicine-01.question: ৩৩) ‘Corkscrew hairs’ found in
Medicine-01.exp:
“Corkscrew hairs” are a classic dermatological feature of Vitamin C deficiency (Scurvy).

Mechanism:

  • Vitamin C is required for collagen synthesis (cofactor for hydroxylation of proline and lysine).

  • Defective collagen formation affects hair follicles and connective tissue.

  • This causes:

    • Corkscrew hairs ✅

    • Perifollicular haemorrhage

    • Easy bruising

    • Bleeding gums

    • Poor wound healing

Other options:

  • Vitamin A deficiency: Causes night blindness, xerophthalmia, and follicular hyperkeratosis, but not corkscrew hairs.

  • Severe malnutrition: Can cause hair changes (thin, brittle hair) but corkscrew hairs are specifically linked to Vitamin C deficiency.

  • Vitamin B1 deficiency: Causes beriberi and neurological/cardiac manifestations.

Exam Pearl:
Corkscrew hairs + bleeding gums + poor wound healing → Vitamin C deficiency (Scurvy).
(Ref: Davidson’s Principles & Practice of Medicine, 23rd ed., p. 692)

Medicine-01.question: ৩৪) Which nutrition toxicity can lead to milk alkali syndrome?
Medicine-01.exp:
Milk-alkali syndrome occurs due to excessive intake of calcium, usually with calcium carbonate-containing supplements and high calcium intake.

Mechanism:

  • Excess calcium ingestion → hypercalcaemia

  • Increased calcium absorption → metabolic alkalosis

  • Reduced renal calcium excretion → worsening hypercalcaemia

Classical triad:

  1. Hypercalcaemia

  2. Metabolic alkalosis

  3. Renal impairment

Other options:

  • Iodine: Excess can cause thyroid dysfunction (e.g., iodine-induced hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism), not milk-alkali syndrome.

  • Arsenic: Causes toxicity with neuropathy, GI symptoms, and skin changes.

  • Zinc: Excess causes copper deficiency and GI symptoms.

Exam Pearl:
Milk-alkali syndrome = Excess calcium (usually calcium carbonate) → Hypercalcaemia + metabolic alkalosis + renal failure.

Medicine-01.question: ৩৫) Which vitamin deficiency is seen in carcinoid syndrome?
Medicine-01.exp:
Carcinoid syndrome causes niacin (Vitamin B3) deficiency due to excessive conversion of tryptophan into serotonin.

Mechanism:

  • Normally, tryptophan is used for niacin synthesis.

  • In carcinoid syndrome, tumour cells produce large amounts of serotonin from tryptophan.

  • This diverts tryptophan away from niacin production → niacin deficiency (pellagra).

Features of niacin deficiency:

  • Dermatitis

  • Diarrhoea

  • Dementia

  • (Classical 3 Ds)

Other options:

  • Thiamine deficiency: Causes beriberi and Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

  • Riboflavin deficiency: Causes cheilosis, glossitis, and corneal vascularization.

  • Pyridoxine deficiency: Causes neuropathy, dermatitis, and sideroblastic anaemia.

Exam Pearl:
Carcinoid syndrome → Tryptophan diverted to serotonin → Niacin deficiency → Pellagra (3 Ds).

Medicine-01.question: ৩৬) Iodine is rich in
Medicine-01.exp:
Edible seaweeds are one of the richest dietary sources of iodine.

Mechanism:

  • Seaweeds accumulate iodine from seawater.

  • They contain high concentrations of iodine required for:

    • Thyroid hormone synthesis (T3 and T4)

    • Normal metabolism and growth

Other options:

  • Liver: Rich in vitamin A, iron, and other nutrients, but not a major iodine source.

  • Shellfish: Contains iodine, but generally less concentrated than seaweeds.

  • Seafood: A good source of iodine, but edible seaweeds have the highest iodine content.

Exam Pearl:
Richest natural source of iodine → Edible seaweeds (kelp).
Iodine deficiency → Goitre + hypothyroidism + impaired growth/development.

Medicine-01.question: ৩৭) Which deficiency leads to keshan’sdisease?
Medicine-01.exp:
Keshan disease is caused by selenium deficiency.

Mechanism:

  • Selenium is an essential component of glutathione peroxidase, an antioxidant enzyme.

  • Selenium deficiency increases oxidative damage to cardiac myocytes.

  • This leads to Keshan disease, a form of endemic cardiomyopathy.

Features:

  • Dilated cardiomyopathy

  • Heart failure

  • Arrhythmias

  • Mainly seen in selenium-deficient regions

Other options:

  • Vitamin B6: Deficiency causes neuropathy, dermatitis, and sideroblastic anaemia.

  • Fluoride: Deficiency affects teeth and bones; excess causes fluorosis.

  • Vitamin C: Deficiency causes scurvy (bleeding gums, corkscrew hairs, poor wound healing).

Exam Pearl:
Selenium deficiency → Keshan disease (endemic cardiomyopathy).
Selenium excess → Selenosis (hair/nail changes, garlic breath)

Medicine-01.question: ৩৮) Biochemical assessment of vitamin B2 deficiency is assessed by
Medicine-01.option3: Red blood cell glutathione reductase activity
Medicine-01.exp:
Vitamin B2 (Riboflavin) deficiency is assessed biochemically by measuring red blood cell (RBC) glutathione reductase activity.

Mechanism:

  • Riboflavin is the precursor of FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) and FMN (flavin mononucleotide).

  • FAD acts as a coenzyme for glutathione reductase.

  • In riboflavin deficiency:

    • RBC glutathione reductase activity decreases.

    • The erythrocyte glutathione reductase activation coefficient (EGRAC) is used as a sensitive marker.

Other options:

  • Erythrocyte transaminase activation coefficient → Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) deficiency.

  • Serum tocopherol : cholesterol ratio → Vitamin E status assessment.

  • RBC transketolase activity → Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency.

Exam Pearl:
Vitamin B1 → ↓ RBC transketolase activity
Vitamin B2 → ↓ RBC glutathione reductase activity (EGRAC)
Vitamin B6 → ↑ Erythrocyte transaminase activation coefficient

Medicine-01.question: ৩৯) Gastric and duodenal ulcer can be differentiated from erosion on the basis of penetration into
Medicine-01.exp:
The key difference between a gastric/duodenal ulcer and an erosion is the depth of mucosal injury.

  • Ulcer 

    • Extends through the muscularis mucosa and penetrates into the submucosa or deeper layers, often reaching the muscularis propria.

  • Erosion 

    • A superficial mucosal defect that does not extend beyond the muscularis mucosa.

Therefore, penetration into the muscularis propria indicates a true peptic ulcer rather than an erosion.

Other options:

  • Lamina propria: Too superficial; seen in mucosal injury/erosion.

  • Muscularis mucosa: Erosions are limited up to this layer.

  • Submucosa: Ulcers may involve this layer, but the classic differentiating depth is extension beyond muscularis mucosa into deeper layers.

Exam Pearl:
Erosion → mucosa only (does not cross muscularis mucosa).
Peptic ulcer → penetrates beyond muscularis mucosa (may reach muscularis propria).

Medicine-01.question: ৪০) Which remains the most important part of the clinical decision-making process?
Medicine-01.exp:
History taking remains the most important part of the clinical decision-making process.

Reason:

  • A well-taken history provides the majority of diagnostic information and helps to:

    • Identify the patient’s main problem

    • Formulate differential diagnoses

    • Decide appropriate examination and investigations

    • Guide management decisions

Other options:

  • General examination: Important for identifying signs of systemic disease, but usually follows history.

  • Systemic examination: Helps confirm clinical findings and narrow diagnosis.

  • Investigation report: Supports or confirms a diagnosis but should not replace clinical assessment.

Exam Pearl:
Clinical diagnosis begins with history → examination → investigations.
History is the cornerstone of clinical decision-making.

Medicine-01.question: ৪১) Which enzyme is more specific for hepatocellular damage
Medicine-01.exp:
ALT is more specific for hepatocellular damage compared with other liver enzymes.

Mechanism:

  • ALT is mainly present in hepatocytes and is released into blood when liver cells are injured.

  • It is a better marker of hepatocellular injury (e.g., acute viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury).

Other options:

  • AST: Present in liver but also found in heart, skeletal muscle, and other tissues, so it is less specific.

  • ALP: Mainly indicates cholestasis or biliary obstruction (also found in bone).

  • GGT: Indicates cholestasis and is useful for confirming hepatic origin of raised ALP; also induced by alcohol and drugs.

Exam Pearl:
Hepatocellular injury → ALT ↑ (most specific)
Cholestasis → ALP ↑ + GGT ↑.

Medicine-01.question: ৪২) Which is the best means of detecting ascites
Medicine-01.exp:
Ultrasonography (USG) is the best initial and most commonly used method for detecting ascites.

Advantages:

  • Highly sensitive for detecting even small amounts of free fluid

  • Non-invasive

  • Easily available

  • No radiation exposure

  • Helps assess the amount and distribution of ascitic fluid

Other options:

  • X-ray: May show signs of large ascites (e.g., increased abdominal density, bowel loop displacement) but is not sensitive.

  • CT: Can detect ascites and provide detailed abdominal imaging, but it is not the first-line test.

  • MRI: Not routinely used for ascites detection due to cost and limited availability.

Exam Pearl:
Best initial investigation for ascites → USG.
Ascitic fluid analysis → Diagnostic paracentesis (gold standard for determining cause).

Medicine-01.question: ৪৩) ‘Constructional apraxia’ occurs due to damage in
Medicine-01.exp:
Constructional apraxia occurs due to damage to the non-dominant parietal lobe (usually the right parietal lobe).

Mechanism:

  • The non-dominant parietal cortex is responsible for:

    • Visuospatial processing

    • Perception of spatial relationships

    • Integration of visual information for construction tasks

  • Damage leads to inability to copy drawings, assemble objects, or construct shapes despite normal motor function.

Clinical examples:

  • Difficulty copying a clock face

  • Inability to draw geometric figures

  • Impaired dressing skills (dressing apraxia)

Other options:

  • Dominant parietal lobe: Causes Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation) and ideomotor apraxia.

  • Temporal lobe lesions: More related to memory, language, and auditory processing.

Exam Pearl:
Constructional apraxia → Right (non-dominant) parietal lobe lesion.
Dominant parietal lesion → Gerstmann syndrome + ideomotor apraxia.

Medicine-01.question: ৪৪) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension may be confirmed by
Medicine-01.exp:
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) is confirmed by lumbar puncture demonstrating raised cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) opening pressure with normal CSF composition.

Diagnostic criteria include:

  • Symptoms/signs of raised intracranial pressure (e.g., headache, papilloedema)

  • Normal brain imaging (MRI ± MR venography to exclude mass lesion or venous thrombosis)

  • Raised CSF opening pressure on lumbar puncture ✅

  • Normal CSF analysis

Other options:

  • MRI: Important to exclude secondary causes (tumour, hydrocephalus, venous sinus thrombosis), but does not confirm IIH.

  • EEG: Used for seizure disorders; not useful in IIH.

  • PET CT: Not used for diagnosis of IIH.

Exam Pearl:
Idiopathic intracranial hypertension → Diagnosis confirmed by raised CSF opening pressure on lumbar puncture.
MRI is for exclusion; LP confirms.

Medicine-01.question: ৪৫) Test to demonstrate anatomy of pancreas prior to surgery
Medicine-01.exp:
MRCP is the preferred non-invasive investigation to demonstrate the anatomy of the pancreas and pancreaticobiliary tree prior to surgery.

Advantages:

  • Provides detailed anatomical visualization of:

    • Pancreatic duct

    • Bile ducts

    • Pancreatic lesions

    • Ductal obstruction or anomalies

  • Non-invasive and does not require contrast injection into ducts.

Other options:

  • ERCP: Provides excellent ductal imaging but is invasive and mainly used for therapeutic procedures (stone extraction, stenting, biopsy), not routine preoperative anatomy mapping.

  • USG: Useful as an initial test for gallstones, biliary dilation, and pancreatic masses, but limited by bowel gas and obesity.

  • CT: Excellent for pancreatic masses, staging, and complications of pancreatitis, but MRCP is better for ductal anatomy.

Exam Pearl:
Preoperative pancreatic duct anatomy → MRCP.
ERCP → mainly therapeutic, not first-line diagnostic.

Medicine-01.question: ৪৬) Which type of melanoma is more common in dark skinned people ?
Medicine-01.exp:
Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM) is the most common type of melanoma seen in dark-skinned individuals.

Features:

  • Occurs on acral sites:

    • Palms

    • Soles

    • Nail beds (subungual region)

  • Not related to sun exposure.

  • More common in people with darker skin pigmentation (e.g., African, Asian, and Hispanic populations).

Other options:

  • Superficial spreading melanoma: Most common melanoma type overall, especially in fair-skinned populations.

  • Lentigo maligna melanoma: Usually occurs on chronically sun-exposed skin in elderly fair-skinned individuals (face, neck).

  • Subungual melanoma: A subtype/location of acral lentiginous melanoma involving the nail unit, but ALM is the broader recognized type.

Exam Pearl:
Dark skin → Acral lentiginous melanoma.
Most common melanoma overall → Superficial spreading melanoma.

Medicine-01.question: ৪৭) In subacute thyroiditis radio iodine uptake is
Medicine-01.exp:
MRCP is the preferred test to demonstrate the anatomy of the pancreas and pancreaticobiliary ducts before surgery.

Why MRCP:

  • It is non-invasive and provides detailed images of:

    • Pancreatic duct

    • Common bile duct

    • Pancreaticobiliary anatomy

    • Ductal obstruction or anomalies

Other options:

  • ERCP: Provides excellent duct visualization but is invasive and mainly used for therapeutic purposes (stone extraction, stenting, biopsy), not routine preoperative mapping.

  • USG: Initial screening test for gallstones and pancreatic abnormalities, but limited for detailed anatomy.

  • CT: Useful for pancreatic masses, staging, and complications, but less suitable for detailed ductal anatomy.

Exam Pearl:
Preoperative demonstration of pancreatic duct anatomy → MRCP.
ERCP → Diagnostic + therapeutic, mainly therapeutic nowadays.

Medicine-01.question: ৪৮) Which channel abnormalities occur in hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis?
Medicine-01.exp:
Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis (HyperPP) is caused by abnormalities in the voltage-gated sodium (Na⁺) channels of skeletal muscle.

Mechanism:

  • It is usually due to mutation in the SCN4A gene, which encodes the skeletal muscle voltage-gated sodium channel (Nav1.4).

  • Defective sodium channel inactivation causes persistent sodium influx.

  • This leads to abnormal muscle membrane excitability and episodes of transient muscle weakness/paralysis, often triggered by:

    • Rest after exercise

    • High potassium intake

    • Fasting

Other options:

  • Magnesium channel abnormality: Not associated with HyperPP.

  • Potassium channel abnormality: Seen in some other periodic paralysis disorders, but classic HyperPP is a sodium channel disorder.

  • Chloride channel abnormality: Associated with myotonia congenita (CLCN1 mutation).

Exam Pearl:
Hyperkalaemic periodic paralysis → SCN4A mutation → Voltage-gated Na⁺ channel defect.
Hypokalaemic periodic paralysis → Ca²⁺ channel (CACNA1S) / Na⁺ channel abnormalities.

Medicine-01.question: ৪৯) Which of the following conditions can cause hyponatremia?
Medicine-01.exp:
Hypothyroidism can cause hyponatremia, especially in severe cases.

Mechanism:

  • Low thyroid hormone levels reduce cardiac output and renal blood flow.

  • This decreases renal water clearance.

  • Increased ADH (antidiuretic hormone) activity causes water retention → dilutional hyponatremia.

Other options:

  • Hyperthyroidism: Usually does not cause hyponatremia.

  • Cushing’s disease: Causes excess cortisol, which has mineralocorticoid effects → sodium retention and may cause hypertension, not hyponatremia.

  • Pheochromocytoma: Causes catecholamine excess with hypertension and does not typically cause hyponatremia.

Exam Pearl:
Endocrine causes of hyponatremia → Hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (↓ cortisol).
Severe hypothyroidism → impaired free water excretion → dilutional hyponatremia.

Medicine-01.question: ৫০) Which of the following is a feature of Behçet’s syndrome?
Medicine-01.exp:
Behçet’s syndrome is a multisystem vasculitis classically characterized by the triad of:

  1. Recurrent oral aphthous ulcers ✅

  2. Recurrent genital ulcers ✅

  3. Ocular inflammation (uveitis with hypopyon) ✅

Mechanism:

  • Behçet’s disease causes inflammation of small and large blood vessels.

  • Eye involvement may include anterior uveitis, which can produce hypopyon (layering of inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber).

Other clinical features:

  • Skin lesions (erythema nodosum, acneiform lesions)

  • Positive pathergy test

  • Arthritis

  • Neurological and vascular complications

Exam Pearl:
Behçet syndrome = Oral ulcers + Genital ulcers + Uveitis (Hypopyon).
Classic triad → All of the above.
